content: Two controlled, multinational, multicenter studies (Studies 300 and 305) were conducted to evaluate the efficacy of tigecycline in comparison to vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours) combined with aztreonam (2 g intravenously every 12 hours) for a duration of 5 to 14 days. Tigecycline was administered as a 100 mg intravenous initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours. These studies enrolled patients with complicated deep soft tissue infections, including wound infections and cellulitis (≥10 cm, requiring surgery or drainage, or associated with complicated underlying disease), major abscesses, infected ulcers, and burns. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical response at the test of cure (TOC) visit in two co-primary populations: clinically evaluable (CE) and clinical modified intent-to-treat (c-mITT) patients. Clinical cure rates at TOC by pathogen in microbiologically evaluable patients are detailed in the study results. Tigecycline was also evaluated in adults for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multinational, multicenter studies (Studies 301 and 306). In these studies, tigecycline (100 mg intravenous initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours) was compared to imipenem/cilastatin (500 mg intravenously every 6 hours) for 5 to 14 days. Patients with complicated diagnoses such as appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, gastric or duodenal perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, intestinal perforation, and peritonitis were included. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical response at the TOC visit in the co-primary populations of microbiologically evaluable (ME) and microbiologic modified intent-to-treat (m-mITT) patients. Clinical cure rates at TOC by pathogen in microbiologically evaluable patients are presented in the study results. For community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP), tigecycline was evaluated in adults in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multinational, multicenter studies (Studies 308 and 313). Tigecycline (100 mg intravenous initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours) was compared to levofloxacin (500 mg intravenously every 12 or 24 hours). In one study (Study 308), after at least 3 days of intravenous therapy, a switch to oral levofloxacin (500 mg daily) was allowed for both treatment arms, with total therapy lasting 7 to 14 days. Patients requiring hospitalization and intravenous therapy for CABP were enrolled. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical response at the TOC visit in the co-primary populations of clinically evaluable (CE) and clinical modified intent-to-treat (c-mITT) patients. Clinical cure rates at TOC by pathogen in microbiologically evaluable patients are detailed in the study results. A post-hoc analysis was conducted to further evaluate the treatment effect of tigecycline in CABP patients at higher risk of mortality, for whom the treatment effect of antibiotics is supported by historical evidence. The higher-risk group included CABP patients from the two studies with any of the following factors: age ≥50 years, PSI score ≥3, or Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia. The results of this analysis are presented in the study findings. Among the higher-risk group, age ≥50 years was the most common risk factor. Tigecycline for injection is supplied in single-dose 5 mL or 10 mL glass vials, each containing 50 mg of tigecycline as a lyophilized powder for reconstitution. It should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). Patients should be counseled that tigecycline, like other antibacterial drugs, should only be used to treat bacterial infections. It is not effective against viral infections (e.g., the common cold). Patients should be informed that even if they feel better early in the course of therapy, the medication should be taken exactly as directed. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance, making future infections harder to treat with tigecycline or other antibacterial drugs. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients should be advised to contact their physician if they develop watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even as late as two or more months after completing the antibiotic course. The interaction between alcohol and tigecycline has not been established. Patients should consult their physician regarding the effects of consuming alcohol while taking this medication.
